subject: history_social
passage: Historians often estimate how many people in a past society could read by counting the share of brides and grooms who signed their names in marriage registers rather than making a mark. The method assumes that people who learned to read also learned to write. In eighteenth-century Sweden, however, the Lutheran church required its members to learn to read religious texts, and clergy regularly examined each household's reading ability; writing, by contrast, was neither required by the church nor commonly taught. Applied to Swedish marriage registers from that century, the signature method would therefore most likely ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: show that most Swedes of that time could write as well as read.
choices.B: overstate the share of Swedes who were able to read.
choices.C: be equally unreliable for every European country of that time.
choices.D: understate the share of Swedes who were able to read.

explanation.why: The signature method counts only people who could write. In eighteenth-century Sweden, many people were taught to read but not to write, so many readers would have made a mark instead of signing. Counting signatures would therefore miss those readers.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says writing was not commonly taught, which gives no reason to think most Swedes could write.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This reverses the effect: the method misses readers who could not write; it does not add people who could not read.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The text describes conditions in Sweden only; it does not show that the method fails in the same way everywhere.
explanation.D: Correct. Many Swedes learned to read without learning to write, so they would not appear among the signers, making the count too low.
